summary: Addresses the gap in GMPLS and MPLS-TE networks between completing LSP signaling and the cross-connection actually being programmed. It defines ways to report data path delay for a Label Switched Path. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Finishing the paperwork for a road does not mean it is ready for cars. This memo helps report how long until the road works.

questions: gmpls signaling versus data plane readiness
what is lsp data path delay
is lsp ready after rsvp-te signaling
subtitle: Five metrics for how long an MPLS or GMPLS tunnel really takes to carry traffic after signaling says it is ready.

tldr.problem: When an LSP is set up with RSVP-TE, finishing the signaling does not guarantee that the cross-connections are programmed, yet applications often treat the final Resv message as a sign that the data path works.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines five delay metrics (RRFD, RSRD, PRFD, PSFD, PSRD) that time the gap between a signaling event and the first error-free signal on the data path, plus sampling and statistics rules.
tldr.outcome: Implementers and application designers get a standard way to measure and report data path readiness and failures. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 6777 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2012, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the control plane metrics of RFC 5814.

sections.title: Why Signaling Is Not Enough
sections.content:
A Label Switched Path (LSP) is set up by signaling, and the things that use it are called applications in this RFC: network management systems, components that forward data onto virtual links, or any other user of an LSP. Ideally, once signaling completes, the LSP can carry traffic.

In practice vendors may program the cross-connections in a pipelined manner to shorten the overall provisioning delay, so the data path may not be ready the instant signaling completes. An implementation fault can be worse: if the data plane fails to program the cross-connection and does not tell the control plane, signaling can succeed while the data path never works. A client that treats the arrival of the correct Resv message as proof of connectivity, for example over the User-Network Interface of RFC 4208, may start sending too early and lose data.

These metrics complement the control plane metrics of RFC 5814, and can be used to check implementations against the advice in RFC 6383.
sections.eli5: Imagine a teacher says 'the playground is open' but the swings are not yet bolted down. If you run onto them right away, you get hurt. These metrics measure how long you should really wait.

sections.title: The Five Metrics
sections.content:
The RFC defines five metrics. Each one is a time difference between a signaling event and the moment the data path becomes ready for use:

  • RRFD (Resv Received, Forward Data): from the Resv message reaching the ingress node to the forward data path being ready.
  • RSRD (Resv Sent, Reverse Data): from the egress node sending the Resv message to the reverse data path being ready.
  • PRFD (PATH Received, Forward Data): from the egress node receiving the PATH message to the forward data path being ready.
  • PSFD (PATH Sent, Forward Data): from the ingress node sending the PATH message to the forward data path being ready.
  • PSRD (PATH Sent, Reverse Data): from the ingress node sending the PATH message to the reverse data path being ready.

The forward data path runs from ingress to egress. The reverse data path runs from egress to ingress in a bidirectional LSP. RSRD may be used with RRFD, and PSRD with PSFD, to characterize a bidirectional LSP.
sections.eli5: It is like five stopwatches, each started by a different message in the setup conversation and stopped when the first good test signal gets through.

sections.title: Terms and the Error-Free Signal
sections.content:
Data path delay is the time needed to complete the data path configuration in relation to signaling. It must not be confused with transmission delay, the time to send traffic across the data path.

Readiness is detected with an error-free signal, a data-plane-specific indication of connectivity. For packet switching interfaces, the first error-free packet from one side to the other may be used. For SDH/SONET cross-connects, the disappearance of an alarm can be used. An implementation must choose a signal suited to the technology under test.

The ingress and egress nodes in this RFC are measurement endpoints with both control plane and data plane features. The control plane part talks to the network under test, while the data plane part generates or receives the test signals.
sections.eli5: The 'error-free signal' is the first clean 'hello' that arrives through the pipe. Hearing it proves the pipe really works.

sections.title: How a Singleton Is Defined and Measured
sections.content:
Each metric is defined as a singleton, a single measurement, using the same outline: motivation, name, parameters, units, definition, discussion and methodology. The parameters are the ingress LSR ID, the egress LSR ID and the time T when setup is attempted. The value is a real number of milliseconds or undefined.

For RRFD, the ingress node sends a PATH message, takes timestamp T1 on receiving the last bit of the Resv message, and the egress node takes T2 when it sees the error-free signal. The estimate is T2 minus T1. The other metrics follow the same pattern with different start and stop points.

Several rules apply across the metrics. If no error-free signal arrives within a threshold, the value MUST be treated as undefined and the threshold MUST be reported. If LSP setup fails, the value MUST NOT be counted. If an error-free signal appears before the PATH message is sent, an error MUST be reported and the measurement SHOULD terminate.
sections.eli5: Start the stopwatch at one message, stop it when the first clean signal shows up. If nothing shows up in time, write 'no answer' instead of a number.

sections.title: Accuracy and Negative Values
sections.content:
Each metric has a discussion of what limits its accuracy. RRFD, RSRD and PSFD depend on the clock resolution of both endpoints and require clock synchronization between ingress and egress. PRFD and PSRD depend on one endpoint's clock, so synchronization between ingress and egress is not required.

For rate-based checks on Ethernet, the gap between successive frames limits accuracy. The RFC RECOMMENDS small intervals, as long as the injected traffic does not exceed the capacity of the path, and the interval MUST be reported. On low-speed Ethernet interfaces, serializing a large frame takes noticeable time, so small frames are RECOMMENDED.

RRFD can be negative. Some implementations program the cross-connection before sending the PATH message downstream, so the data path may be ready before the Resv message reaches the ingress node. When RRFD is negative, a PRFD measurement is RECOMMENDED to characterize the forward data path further.
sections.eli5: If your stopwatch is a little off, or you only check once in a while, your time will be a bit wrong. Sometimes the road is ready before the paperwork is finished, which gives a negative time.

sections.title: Sampling and Test Cases
sections.content:
To collect many singletons, the RFC defines samples of each metric. Following RFC 2330, it uses Poisson sampling as the example. The parameters include a start time T0, an end time Tf, a rate Lambda in reciprocal milliseconds, the LSP holding time Th, the maximum waiting time for LSP setup Td and the maximum wait for an error-free signal Ts. The value of Ts MUST be reported with the sample.

At each selected time the LSP is set up, the delay is obtained, and the LSP is released after Th. Two typical test cases are described. With no LSP in the network, the result reflects the inherent delay of a device, and the minimum indicates the delay under light load. With a number of LSPs in the network, the result reflects an operational network with considerable load and can serve as a scalability metric.
sections.eli5: Instead of timing the road once, you time it at random moments, once when the town is empty and once when it is busy, so you learn what is typical.

sections.title: Statistics to Report
sections.content:
From a sample the RFC defines statistics to report, considering only finite values. The minimum treats undefined values as infinitely large, so it is undefined if all values are undefined or the sample is empty. The median excludes undefined values and may not be typical when few defined values exist. The percentile is based on the empirical distribution function and also excludes undefined values.

Failures are summarized by two figures. Failure Count is the number of undefined values in a sample. Failure Ratio is the number of undefined values divided by the number of valid values plus undefined values, times 100%. A failure event means signaling completed with no error but no error-free signal was observed.
sections.eli5: After many timings you report the fastest, the middle one, and how often the road never opened at all.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Measurement endpoints behave as normal signaling endpoints, so on the control plane they add no security issues beyond normal LSP provisioning. The parameters must be chosen so that measurements inject only trivial amounts of traffic, since too much can skew results and in extreme cases cause congestion and denial of service.

On the data plane the test signal MUST be consistent with the control plane. For packet switching the injected traffic MUST NOT exceed the rate in the LSP setup request, and for wavelength switching the endpoint MUST use the specified or negotiated lambda with appropriate power. The security considerations of RFC 2205 and RFC 3209 also remain relevant.
sections.eli5: When testing the road, do not send so many toy cars that you cause a traffic jam, and only use the lane you were given.
